requirements: The core contributions of "FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness" have been reproduced, including the tiled forward/backward attention kernel, block-sparse extension, IO-complexity analysis, and all end-to-end training and benchmarking results.

sub_tasks.requirements: The CUDA/PyTorch environment and NVIDIA A100 GPU configuration required to build and run the FlashAttention CUDA kernel are prepared, including compiler toolchain, GPU detection, multi-GPU setup for training runs, and access to the Apex FMHA starting-point code referenced in the Acknowledgments.
GPU hardware discovery and validation utilities are in place so that the codebase can confirm it is running on the NVIDIA A100 platform assumed throughout the paper (Section 2.1, Section 4).

Code has been implemented that queries the CUDA device via a PyTorch or CUDA runtime call (e.g., torch.cuda.get_device_name / cudaGetDeviceProperties) and asserts that the detected GPU name contains 'A100', failing loudly with a descriptive error if run on any other device.

Code has been implemented that reads the GPU's total HBM capacity and confirms it is either ~40 GB or ~80 GB (matching the A100 40GB/80GB SKUs described in Section 2.1), and records the value in a run-log or environment report.

A configuration constant or query defines the on-chip SRAM size per streaming multiprocessor as 192 KB (Section 2.1) and the number of SMs as 108 for A100, and this value is what the FlashAttention kernel uses to select the block sizes B_r and B_c at build/launch time.
A CUDA/PyTorch build environment is set up such that the custom FlashAttention CUDA kernel can be compiled and loaded from Python.

Code has been implemented (e.g., environment.yml, requirements.txt, Dockerfile, or install script) that installs a specific CUDA toolkit version compatible with A100 (compute capability 8.0), a matching PyTorch build with CUDA support, and ninja / a C++17-capable host compiler needed to JIT-compile CUDA extensions.

A setup.py / CMake / torch.utils.cpp_extension.load configuration exists that compiles the FlashAttention CUDA sources with -gencode targeting sm_80 (A100) and links against the PyTorch runtime, producing a Python-importable extension module.

The compiled FlashAttention extension can be imported and a smoke-test forward call on a small (Q,K,V) tensor on an A100 GPU returns a tensor of the expected shape and dtype (fp16/bf16) without raising a CUDA error, confirming the toolchain is functional end-to-end.
The 8×A100 multi-GPU training configuration used for BERT-large, GPT-2, and long-context runs (Tables 1, 2, 4) is set up.

Code has been implemented that initializes a distributed data-parallel (or equivalent) training group across 8 GPUs (e.g., torch.distributed with NCCL backend) and verifies the world size is 8 A100 devices before starting a training run.

The training entry point exposes a launcher (torchrun / mpirun / bash script) that maps one process per GPU across the 8 A100s and passes rank/local-rank correctly, so the BERT and GPT-2 training scripts described in Section 4.1 can be launched with a single command.
The Apex FMHA reference implementation used as a starting point (Acknowledgments) is made available to the build so the kernel can inherit its warp-level MMA layout and pipeline structure.

Code or documentation has been implemented that pins a specific commit of NVIDIA/apex (containing apex/contrib/csrc/fmha) and either clones it as a submodule or copies the relevant fmha C++/CUDA headers into the project's third_party/ directory prior to compiling FlashAttention.
The environment is captured reproducibly so that every experiment reported in the paper can be re-run against the same CUDA/PyTorch/Apex versions.

A reproduce.sh (or equivalent) script exists at the repo root that (a) verifies A100 GPU presence, (b) builds the CUDA extension, and (c) runs at least one FlashAttention forward+backward correctness check before dispatching downstream experiments, exiting non-zero on any failure.

All datasets (Wikipedia for BERT, OpenWebText for GPT-2, Long-Range Arena tasks, MIMIC-III, ECtHR, Path-X, Path-256) and starting checkpoints (MLPerf BERT init, pretrained RoBERTa, Path-64 pretrained transformer) required by the paper's experiments are obtained and prepared.
Language modeling training corpora for BERT-large (Wikipedia) and GPT-2 (OpenWebText) are acquired and preprocessed into the tokenized, packed formats used in Table 1, Table 2, and Table 4.
Code has been implemented that downloads/extracts a Wikipedia dump and prepares the sentence-segmented text corpus used to train BERT-large in Table 1.

Code has been implemented that tokenizes the Wikipedia corpus with the BERT WordPiece vocabulary, packs examples into sequence length 512, and applies the MLM masking protocol expected by the MLPerf 1.1 BERT-large training recipe.
Code has been implemented that downloads the OpenWebText corpus (Gokaslan et al.) used for GPT-2 training in Table 2 and Table 4.
Code has been implemented that tokenizes OpenWebText with the GPT-2 BPE tokenizer and produces training/validation shards of concatenated token ids suitable for causal language modeling.

Code has been implemented that packs the tokenized OpenWebText stream into fixed-context training samples at context lengths 1024, 2048, and 4096 tokens (as required by the Table 4 long-context GPT-2 runs).

The five standard Long-Range Arena tasks (ListOps, Text, Retrieval, Image, Pathfinder) are obtained and preprocessed to the sequence-length / tokenization conventions of Tay et al. [80] used in Table 3.
Code has been implemented that loads the LRA ListOps split and prepares tokenized sequences at the LRA-specified sequence length used for the Table 3 experiments.
Code has been implemented that loads the LRA Text (byte-level IMDb) task and produces byte-tokenized sequences at the LRA sequence length used in Table 3.
Code has been implemented that loads the LRA Retrieval (byte-level ACL matching) task and prepares paired-sequence inputs at the LRA-specified length used in Table 3.
Code has been implemented that loads the LRA Image task (CIFAR-10 rendered as grayscale pixel sequences of length 1024) as used in Table 3.
Code has been implemented that loads the LRA Pathfinder-32 task (128x128 -> length 1024 pixel sequences) used in Table 3.
The extended-length Pathfinder tasks Path-X (sequence length 16,384) and Path-256 (sequence length 65,536) used in Table 6 are prepared as flat pixel sequences per image.
Code has been implemented that generates or loads Path-X (Pathfinder-128) images and flattens them one pixel at a time into token sequences of length 16,384 for the Table 6 experiment.
Code has been implemented that generates or loads Path-256 (Pathfinder-256) images and flattens them into token sequences of length 65,536 for the Table 6 experiment.

The long-document classification datasets MIMIC-III (discharge summaries with multi-label ICD codes) and ECtHR (legal cases with allegedly violated Convention articles) required for Table 5 are acquired and prepared.

Code has been implemented that obtains (via credentialed download or documented access script) the MIMIC-III discharge-summary long-document classification dataset with its multi-label targets, as used in Table 5.

The prepared MIMIC-III split matches the paper's reported document-length statistics: mean length ~2,395 tokens and maximum length 14,562 tokens under the tokenizer used for the RoBERTa experiments in Table 5.

The prepared ECtHR split matches the paper's reported document-length statistics: mean length ~2,197 tokens and maximum length 49,392 tokens under the tokenizer used for the RoBERTa experiments in Table 5.

All pretrained starting checkpoints used by the paper's experiments (MLPerf BERT-large init for Table 1, pretrained RoBERTa for Table 5, Path-64 pretrained transformer for Table 6) are downloaded and made loadable.

Code has been implemented that obtains the MLPerf 1.1 BERT-large initialization checkpoint (Nvidia MLPerf reference) so that both the FlashAttention and reference-baseline BERT-large runs in Table 1 start from an identical set of weights.
Code has been implemented that downloads the pretrained RoBERTa checkpoint (Liu et al. [56]) used as the base model for the MIMIC-III and ECtHR long-document classification experiments in Table 5.

Code has been implemented that produces the Path-64 pretrained transformer checkpoint (either downloaded or trained via a provided recipe on Pathfinder-32/64) used as the initialization that is spatially interpolated for the Path-X transfer in Table 6.

Code has been implemented that extends the RoBERTa positional embeddings to the long context lengths used in Table 5 (up to 16,384 tokens on MIMIC-III and up to 8,192 on ECtHR) by repeating/tiling the pretrained positional embeddings following Beltagy et al. [3].

The tiled fused-kernel forward pass of FlashAttention (Algorithm 1/2) is implemented in CUDA, including block-size selection, online softmax statistics (m, ℓ), scaling, masking, and dropout, matching the algorithm specification.

A single fused CUDA kernel implements the FlashAttention forward pass and is exposed to Python (e.g. via a PyTorch extension) so that all attention operations happen in one kernel launch without materializing S or P in HBM.

Code has been implemented containing a CUDA source file (e.g. fmha_fwd_kernel.cu) that defines a __global__ FlashAttention forward kernel, compiled as a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension (setup.py or CMake build) that produces a loadable Python module.

Code has been implemented exposing a Python-callable forward function whose signature accepts Q, K, V tensors of shape (batch, heads, N, d), a softmax scaling constant τ, an optional attention mask, and a dropout probability p_drop, matching the inputs required by Algorithm 2.

Code has been implemented so that the forward function returns the output tensor O of shape (batch, heads, N, d) together with the softmax statistics ℓ and m and the PRNG state R (as specified in Algorithm 2 line 19), packaged for use by the backward pass.

A behavioral test verifies that invoking the FlashAttention forward launches exactly one CUDA kernel (or a small fixed number, not O(N)) and does not allocate any intermediate tensor of shape (N,N), confirming the fused, non-materializing design.
Block sizes Bc and Br are chosen from the on-chip SRAM budget M and head dimension d exactly as prescribed by Algorithm 1/2 line 2.

Code has been implemented that queries or is parameterized by the on-chip SRAM size M (per streaming multiprocessor) used to derive block sizes rather than hard-coding a single block size for all configurations.
Code has been implemented that computes the column block size as Bc = ceil(M / (4·d)), matching the formula in Algorithm 1 line 1 / Algorithm 2 line 2.
Code has been implemented that computes the row block size as Br = min(ceil(M / (4·d)), d), matching the second half of the block-size formula in Algorithm 1/2.

A unit test asserts that for representative (M, d) pairs (e.g. M ≈ 100 KB, d ∈ {64, 128}) the chosen (Bc, Br) satisfy Bc·d + Br·d + Br·Bc ≤ M so that Q_i, K_j, V_j blocks plus S_ij fit into SRAM as required by Section 3.1.

The kernel correctly manages HBM/SRAM data movement: initializing global buffers, dividing inputs into blocks, and loading K_j/V_j and Q_i/O_i/ℓ_i/m_i tiles into on-chip SRAM as in Algorithm 2 lines 3-9.

Code has been implemented that initializes the output O to zeros of shape (N,d), the softmax normalizer ℓ to zeros of length N, and the running max m to -∞ of length N in HBM prior to entering the loops (Algorithm 2 line 3).

Code has been implemented that partitions Q into Tr = ceil(N/Br) row blocks of size Br × d and K, V into Tc = ceil(N/Bc) column blocks of size Bc × d, and correspondingly partitions O, ℓ, and m into Tr blocks (Algorithm 2 lines 4-5).
Code has been implemented that, in the outer loop iteration j, explicitly loads a K_j tile and a V_j tile from HBM into shared memory / registers before the inner loop begins (Algorithm 2 line 7).
Code has been implemented that, in the inner loop iteration i, loads Q_i, O_i, ℓ_i, and m_i from HBM into on-chip storage before performing the block computation (Algorithm 2 line 9).

A behavioral test with a mock or instrumented memory subsystem (or CUDA profiler counters) confirms that each K_j/V_j tile is loaded from HBM exactly once per outer-loop iteration, and Q_i/O_i are streamed through in the inner loop, matching the two-level tiling pattern of Algorithm 1.
The double-nested loop structure of Algorithm 2 (outer over K,V blocks; inner over Q blocks) is implemented, with the outer index j spanning [1,Tc] and inner index i spanning [1,Tr].

Code has been implemented in which the OUTER loop iterates over K/V column blocks (index j = 1..Tc) and the INNER loop iterates over Q row blocks (index i = 1..Tr), matching Algorithm 2 lines 6-8 (and not the reversed ordering).

Code has been implemented that correctly handles the case N mod Br ≠ 0 or N mod Bc ≠ 0 by using appropriate boundary masking on the final tile so that no out-of-bounds elements contaminate the softmax statistics.

A behavioral test verifies that varying (N, Br, Bc) — e.g. non-multiple-of-block sequence lengths and small vs. large block sizes — still produces an output O numerically equal to the standard attention reference (up to FP16 tolerance).
The per-block scaled QK^T product S_ij = τ · Q_i · K_j^T is computed on-chip in the inner loop (Algorithm 2 line 10).
Code has been implemented that performs the per-block matmul S_ij = Q_i · K_j^T of shapes (Br × d) × (d × Bc) → (Br × Bc) using on-chip storage (registers/shared memory), without a round-trip to HBM.

Code has been implemented that applies the softmax scaling factor τ (typically 1/√d) to the QK^T block, either fused into the matmul or applied to S_ij immediately after, so that downstream softmax operates on the scaled scores.

A behavioral test compares the intermediate S_ij block produced by the kernel (via a debug hook or by disabling subsequent softmax) against the reference (τ · Q · K^T)[i_block, j_block] and asserts elementwise agreement within FP16 tolerance.
The attention mask (padding / causal / user-supplied) is applied to the on-chip S_ij block before softmax, as described in Algorithm 2 line 11 and Appendix B.3.
Code has been implemented that accepts a masking specification (padding mask, causal flag, or arbitrary boolean mask) and applies it elementwise to the on-chip S_ij tile inside the fused kernel.

Code has been implemented that sets masked positions of S_ij to -∞ (or a sufficiently negative sentinel) before the rowmax/exp step so their contribution to softmax is exactly zero, per the definition of `mask` in Appendix B.3.

A behavioral test with a padding mask (some rows or columns entirely masked out) verifies that the kernel's output for the masked positions matches the reference attention output computed with the same mask, within FP16 tolerance.
The online softmax statistics update rule of Algorithm 1/2 (lines 10-11) is implemented, tracking the running rowmax m_i and rowsum ℓ_i across successive K,V blocks.
Code has been implemented that computes the per-tile rowmax m̃_ij = rowmax(S_ij^masked) ∈ R^{Br} on chip using warp/block reductions before subtracting it from S_ij.
Code has been implemented that computes P̃_ij = exp(S_ij^masked − m̃_ij) elementwise on chip using the shifted values (guaranteeing numerical stability of the exponentials).
Code has been implemented that computes ℓ̃_ij = rowsum(P̃_ij) ∈ R^{Br} on chip using warp/block reductions.
Code has been implemented that updates the running rowmax as m_i^new = max(m_i, m̃_ij) elementwise per row, matching Algorithm 2 line 12.
Code has been implemented that updates the running rowsum as ℓ_i^new = e^{m_i − m_i^new}·ℓ_i + e^{m̃_ij − m_i^new}·ℓ̃_ij, exactly matching the algebraic-aggregation formula in Algorithm 2 line 12.

A unit test constructs a small (N, d) attention problem, runs the kernel one K/V block at a time (or asserts on the exposed intermediate ℓ, m), and verifies that after processing all Tc blocks the final (m, ℓ) equals the row-wise max and rowsum of exp(S − m) of the full standard-attention S within FP32 tolerance.
Elementwise dropout with probability p_drop is fused into the kernel using a saved PRNG state, as specified in Algorithm 2 lines 1, 14 and Appendix B.3.

Code has been implemented that initializes and stores a pseudo-random-number-generator state R at the start of the forward pass and writes it to HBM so the backward pass can regenerate the identical dropout mask (Algorithm 2 line 1, Appendix B.4 observation 1).

Code has been implemented that generates a per-element dropout mask on chip from R and forms P̃_ij^dropped = P̃_ij ⊙ Z_ij where entries of Z_ij are 1/(1−p_drop) with probability 1−p_drop and 0 with probability p_drop.

A behavioral test with p_drop = 0 verifies that the kernel output is bit-identical (or within FP16 tolerance) to the same kernel run with dropout disabled, and with p_drop > 0 verifies that the fraction of masked-to-zero entries in P is within a small tolerance of p_drop over many rows.
The output tile O_i is rescaled and accumulated using the previous and new normalization statistics, matching Algorithm 2 line 15.

Code has been implemented that computes the updated output tile O_i ← diag(ℓ_i^new)^{-1} · (diag(ℓ_i) · e^{m_i − m_i^new} · O_i + e^{m̃_ij − m_i^new} · P̃_ij^dropped · V_j) on chip, exactly matching the rescale-and-accumulate formula of Algorithm 2 line 15.
Code has been implemented that writes the updated O_i tile back to HBM at the end of the inner-loop iteration (Algorithm 2 line 15) and writes updated ℓ_i and m_i back to HBM (Algorithm 2 line 16).

A unit test on small (batch, heads, N, d) inputs asserts that the final O returned by the FlashAttention forward matches the reference softmax(τ·Q·K^T)·V (with mask and dropout disabled) to within a max-abs error tolerance appropriate to the dtype (e.g. 1e-3 for FP16, 1e-5 for FP32).
The forward kernel saves the auxiliary state required by the backward pass — the softmax normalizers ℓ and m and the PRNG state R — so that Algorithm 4 can recompute S and P from Q,K,V blocks.
Code has been implemented that persists the per-row softmax normalizer ℓ ∈ R^N and running max m ∈ R^N to HBM (or an autograd-saved buffer) at the end of the forward pass.
Code has been implemented that persists the pseudo-random-number-generator state R used during dropout so the backward pass can reproduce the identical dropout mask without storing an O(N²) mask.

A behavioral test invokes the forward pass twice with the same inputs and verifies (a) the returned ℓ, m are byte-identical between runs, and (b) using the saved R the dropout mask can be regenerated to exactly match the mask actually applied in the forward, satisfying the precondition assumed by Algorithm 4.
The kernel is wrapped as a differentiable PyTorch primitive so it can be substituted for standard scaled-dot-product attention in a Transformer.

Code has been implemented that defines a torch.autograd.Function subclass whose forward invokes the FlashAttention CUDA kernel and whose ctx saves Q, K, V, O, ℓ, m, and R for use by the backward, so gradient flow through the operator works in PyTorch.

Code has been implemented providing a user-facing Python wrapper (e.g. flash_attn_func(q, k, v, dropout_p, softmax_scale, causal)) with a signature compatible with a standard attention drop-in, so Transformer models can call it in place of torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention.
The forward pass satisfies the correctness, FLOP, and HBM-access properties claimed for it in Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 of the paper.

An end-to-end numerical-equivalence test asserts that for randomly generated Q, K, V (with N up to ~4096, d ∈ {64,128}) the FlashAttention forward output equals softmax(τ·Q·K^T)·V computed by the standard PyTorch implementation to within FP16 max-abs-error tolerance (e.g. ≤ 5e-3), demonstrating Theorem 1 correctness.

A measured test confirms that the additional (non-input/output) memory allocated by the forward pass grows as O(N) — specifically, the sizes of the persisted ℓ and m are each proportional to N and no O(N²) attention or softmax matrix is allocated — matching the O(N) extra-memory claim of Theorem 1.

A measured microbenchmark using ncu / nvprof HBM traffic counters confirms that the forward kernel's HBM read+write volume scales as Θ(N²·d²/M) with sequence length N (and, correspondingly, as ≈9× fewer HBM bytes than the standard PyTorch attention for GPT-2 sized configurations with d=64, N=1024), matching Theorem 2.

A measured microbenchmark confirms that the FLOP count of the forward pass scales as O(N²·d) with sequence length N (e.g. within ±10% of 2·N²·d·H·B FMA count for batch B and H heads), matching the FLOP claim of Theorem 1 and consistent with the ~75.2 GFLOPs reported for FlashAttention on the GPT-2-medium configuration in Fig. 2 (left).

The FlashAttention backward pass (Algorithm 4) is implemented, using stored softmax normalization statistics (m, ℓ) and saved RNG state to recompute S and P on-chip, producing dQ, dK, dV consistent with standard attention gradients.
Backward kernel structure and Python integration for Algorithm 4 exist and expose the inputs required for recomputation.

Code has been implemented that provides a dedicated CUDA source file for the FlashAttention backward kernel (separate from or paired with the forward kernel) exposing a callable entry point for the autograd Function.

Code has been implemented so that the Python torch.autograd.Function forward saves Q, K, V, O, the softmax statistics ℓ and m, and the pseudo-random number generator state R (Algorithm 2 line 19) into ctx for use by the backward.
The backward autograd entry point accepts dO of shape (batch, heads, N, d) and returns dQ, dK, dV tensors of matching shapes and dtypes to the forward inputs.
The backward kernel uses block sizes Bc = ⌈M/(4d)⌉ and Br = min(⌈M/(4d)⌉, d) matching the forward pass (Algorithm 4 line 2) so that recomputed S_ij blocks align with forward blocks.
The backward implements an outer loop over K/V blocks j∈[1,Tc] and an inner loop over Q blocks i∈[1,Tr] as in Algorithm 4 lines 6–9, matching the block scheduling of the forward.
Code has been implemented so that the build/setup script compiles the backward CUDA kernel and links it into the Python package used by reproduce.sh.
On-chip recomputation of the attention score matrix S and probability matrix P using the saved softmax normalization statistics, as described in Section 3.1 and Algorithm 4.
Code has been implemented so that S_ij = τ · Q_i K_jᵀ is recomputed on-chip from Q_i and K_j blocks loaded to SRAM (Algorithm 4 line 11) and never materialized to HBM.

Code has been implemented so that the masking function (e.g., causal mask, key-padding mask) is applied to S_ij to produce S_ij^masked before exponentiation (Algorithm 4 line 12), reusing the same mask semantics as the forward.

Code has been implemented so that P_ij is reconstructed on-chip as diag(ℓ_i)^{-1} · exp(S_ij^masked − m_i) using the saved forward statistics ℓ_i and m_i (Algorithm 4 line 13), without loading a stored P matrix from HBM.
A unit test verifies that on a small random input, the on-chip recomputed P_ij block matches the P computed by a reference softmax(QKᵀ · τ) implementation within 1e-5 (fp32) / 1e-3 (fp16) tolerance.
Gradient computation formulas from Appendix B.2 / Appendix B.4 (D_i, dP, dS, dV, dK, dQ) are implemented block-wise on-chip.
Code has been implemented so that D_i is computed as the rowwise dot product dO_i · O_i (Appendix B.4 observation 2, D_i = doᵢᵀ oᵢ), avoiding any full-length reduction over P_i: or dP_i:.
Code has been implemented so that dP_ij = dO_i V_jᵀ is computed on-chip within the (j,i) block iteration (Algorithm 4 line 17 pattern).
Code has been implemented so that dS_ij = P_ij ◦ (dP_ij − D_i) matches the derivation dS_ij = P_ij (dP_ij − D_i) given in Appendix B.2.
Code has been implemented so that dV_j is accumulated as dV_j ← dV_j + (P_ij^{dropped})ᵀ · dO_i (Algorithm 4 line 16) across all i for the current j block.
Code has been implemented so that dK_j is accumulated as dK_j ← dK_j + τ · dS_ijᵀ · Q_i across all i for the current j block, with the softmax scaling τ applied.
Code has been implemented so that dQ_i is accumulated as dQ_i ← dQ_i + τ · dS_ij · K_j across all j visits for the current i block, with the softmax scaling τ applied.
A unit test verifies that on a small random input, the block-computed dS matches a reference full-matrix computation of P ◦ (dP − D) within numerical tolerance.
Cross-block accumulation semantics for dQ, dK, dV correctly handle the dependency that each dQ_i is updated by every j and each dK_j/dV_j by every i.

Code has been implemented so that dQ_i is loaded from HBM to SRAM at the start of each inner iteration and written back to HBM after the update, ensuring accumulation across successive j blocks is not lost.
Code has been implemented so that dK_j and dV_j accumulators are kept in registers/SRAM across the inner loop over i and written to HBM once per j block (Algorithm 4 lines 8, 16, 19).
A behavioral test verifies that two invocations of the backward on the same inputs (with dropout disabled) produce bitwise-identical dQ, dK, dV, confirming deterministic accumulation ordering.
Dropout is handled deterministically in the backward by restoring the saved RNG state and regenerating the same dropout mask used in the forward.

Code has been implemented so that the pseudo-random number generator state R saved by the forward pass is restored at the beginning of the backward pass (Algorithm 4 line 1), avoiding storing an O(N²) dropout mask.
Code has been implemented so that the dropout mask Z_ij regenerated during backward matches (block-for-block) the mask used in the forward for the same (j,i) pair.

Code has been implemented so that the dropout scale 1/(1−p_drop) is applied consistently in both the forward output P^dropped and the backward gradient path (so that inverted-dropout chain rule is preserved).

A behavioral test with p_drop=0.1 and a fixed CUDA RNG seed verifies that FlashAttention backward produces dQ/dK/dV matching a reference PyTorch attention backward that shares the same dropout mask, within fp16 tolerance.
Masking (causal and key-padding) is applied identically in the backward recomputation and yields zero gradient at masked positions.

Code has been implemented so that the same masking function used in the forward is applied to the recomputed S_ij in the backward before softmax reconstruction, keeping recomputed P consistent with the forward.
A behavioral test with a causal mask verifies that gradients flowing through upper-triangular attention positions are exactly zero in dQ, dK, dV.
A behavioral test with a key-padding mask verifies that dK and dV entries corresponding to padded key positions are exactly zero.
Numerical correctness of dQ, dK, dV versus standard attention gradients, matching Theorem 1 (exact attention gradients).

A numerical test verifies that dV produced by FlashAttention backward matches the reference torch.autograd dV for softmax(QKᵀ·τ)V within max abs error 1e-3 in fp16 on a random (batch=2, heads=4, N=256, d=64) input.
A numerical test verifies that dK produced by FlashAttention backward matches the reference torch.autograd dK within max abs error 1e-3 in fp16 on the same random input.
A numerical test verifies that dQ produced by FlashAttention backward matches the reference torch.autograd dQ within max abs error 1e-3 in fp16 on the same random input.
A sweep test verifies gradient correctness across head dimensions d∈{16, 32, 64, 128} against the torch reference.
A sweep test verifies gradient correctness across sequence lengths N∈{128, 512, 2048} against the torch reference.
An end-to-end gradient test uses torch.autograd.gradcheck (or an equivalent finite-difference check in fp64) on a small (N=32, d=16) FlashAttention module and passes.
Backward pass memory footprint reflects the recomputation strategy: no O(N²) intermediates stored in HBM.
Code has been implemented so that the backward never allocates full N×N tensors for P, dP, or dS in HBM; only per-block Br×Bc SRAM tiles are used.

A behavioral test measures peak CUDA memory during backward across N∈{512, 1024, 2048, 4096} at fixed d=64 and confirms it grows linearly (not quadratically) in N beyond the inputs and outputs (Theorem 1 O(N) extra memory).

The block-sparse FlashAttention extension (Algorithm 5) is implemented, accepting a block-sparsity mask (butterfly pattern), skipping zero blocks in both forward and backward passes, and integrating with the same fused-kernel infrastructure.
The block-sparsity mask interface accepts a block-level boolean matrix M ∈ {0,1}^(N/Br × N/Bc) with the block-form structure described in Section 3.3.
Code has been implemented that defines a block-sparsity mask API accepting an integer/boolean tensor of shape (N/Br, N/Bc) with block sizes Br, Bc matching the FlashAttention kernel tile sizes.

The mask expansion routine, when given a block mask M of shape (N/Br, N/Bc), produces the equivalent element-wise mask M̃ ∈ {0,1}^(N×N) satisfying M̃_{k,l} = M_{⌊k/Br⌋, ⌊l/Bc⌋} for validation against a reference dense masked attention.

The block-sparse attention definition applies -∞ to masked positions before softmax (S ⊙ 𝟙_M̃ with -∞ on zero blocks), so that a fully-ones mask reproduces dense FlashAttention output within numerical tolerance (e.g., max abs diff < 1e-3 in fp16).
A butterfly sparsity pattern generator produces the fixed block-sparsity mask used for downstream LRA and long-sequence experiments.

Code has been implemented for a fixed butterfly sparsity pattern generator (per Dao et al. Pixelated Butterfly [17]) that emits a block-level {0,1} mask of shape (N/Br, N/Bc) for arbitrary sequence length N.

The generated butterfly mask has a nonzero-block fraction that scales as O(log N / N) (or the target s used for benchmarking), verified by counting nonzero blocks for at least two sequence lengths (e.g., N=1024 and N=4096).
The generated butterfly mask is symmetric where required for bidirectional attention and includes the diagonal blocks (self-attention within each block), verified by structural inspection.
Block-sparse FlashAttention forward pass (Algorithm 5) is implemented as a modification of Algorithm 1 that skips zero blocks of the sparsity mask.
Code has been implemented that inside the nested (j-outer, i-inner) block loop of Algorithm 5 tests M[i,j] and continues past the S_ij computation, softmax update, and O_i write when M[i,j] == 0.
